tasks.task: perf(v4): lazy ZodError construction Defer $ZodError construction work that a failing safeParse almost never consumes. The message was an eager pretty-printed JSON dump of every issue; it is now an own accessor computed and cached on first read, with a setter preserving plain-assignment semantics. The classic helper methods (format/flatten/addIssue/addIssues/isEmpty) and toString move from nine per-instance property definitions to lazy getters installed once on the shared prototype, each caching its bound closure on first access, so detached usage still works. Measured against the branch point with an A/B harness that loads both revisions into one process (noise floor +/-1.2% on the suite total): failing safeParse -39% to -41%, string formats with 50% invalid input -37% to -40%, whole 11-workload suite -20% to -23%. Success paths are unchanged. Enumeration, serialisation, .format()/.flatten(), treeifyError(), prettifyError(), the Standard Schema surface and the stack trace (which V8 formats lazily, so it still carries the message and the parse call site) are all byte-identical. Two follow-up commits: clear the shared descriptor slots, which otherwise pinned the last error's issues array for the process lifetime, and seed the prototype-install guards with Object.prototype and Error.prototype so `init` on a foreign object cannot shadow an intrinsic toString.
tasks.subject: perf(v4): lazy ZodError construction (#6316)

tasks.task: fix(v4): preserve z.preprocess input narrowing replaced `preprocess()`'s return type `ZodPipe<ZodTransform<A, B>, U>` with `ZodPreprocess<U>`, which pins `def.in` to a bare `$ZodTransform`. Its `I` slot defaulted to `unknown`, so `$ZodPipeInternals` derived the pipe input as `unknown` and the annotated preprocessor argument stopped reaching `z.input`. Thread the argument type through as a second generic on `$ZodPreprocess` and its def/internals, as `$ZodTransform<unknown, I>`. The transform's output stays `unknown` on purpose: `$ZodPipeDef`'s codec-only `transform?` field is typed over `core.output<A>`, so binding it there would make a narrowed `ZodPreprocess` unassignable to the bare `ZodPreprocess`. Type-only; no runtime change. The documented default is unchanged — an un-annotated preprocessor still infers `unknown`.

tasks.task: fix(json-schema): keep preprocess object properties required in input mode * fix(json-schema): keep preprocess object properties required in input mode `z.preprocess(fn, inner)` builds a pipe whose `in` is a transform. A bare transform reports `optin: "optional"` (needed so the preprocessor still runs on absent keys at parse time), and ZodPipe inherits `optin` from its `in`, so the object processor marked preprocessed properties as not-required in `toJSONSchema(..., { io: "input" })` — a regression since v4.4.3 . This contradicts runtime parsing: `z.object({ a: z.preprocess(v => v, z.string()) }).parse({})` rejects the absent `a`. The input shape of a preprocess pipe is its inner `out` schema, so optionality should defer to that inner schema (the v4.4.2 behavior, design of #5929). Resolve `optin` through transform-`in` pipes in the JSON-schema object processor only; runtime optin is untouched. Fixes #5968. * fix(json-schema): keep catch properties required in input mode `$ZodCatch` sets `optin = "optional"` at runtime so the parser lets the catch handler observe an absent key , but its declared input type keeps the key required. `io: "input"` describes the declared type, so resolve past catch the same way this now resolves past a transform-led pipe. flipped this without comment and dropped `"f"` from the `input type` snapshot, reverting the position established in and #5003. Restore both. Also updates the object snapshot added by #6409: a catch over a transforming schema declares a `string` input, so the key is required there too. ---------

tasks.task: fix(from-json-schema): drop redundant inclusive bound for draft-04 exclusive ranges In draft-04 `exclusiveMinimum: true` makes the sibling `minimum` exclusive rather than an independent bound, so the converter emitted one check more than the source schema declares: `.min(5)` alongside `.gt(5)`. The one observable effect is in Zod's own parse output, where an out-of-range value reported two issues instead of one, the second naming a bound the schema does not have. `!== true` leaves the draft-06+ numeric form alone, where `minimum` and `exclusiveMinimum` are legitimately independent.

tasks.task: fix(v4): let the includes(position) pattern match at or after the offset `String.prototype.includes(sub, position)` treats position as a start offset, so it matches at that index or any later one. The pattern this check advertised used `{N}`, which pins the substring to exactly index N, and `z.toJSONSchema()` emitted it verbatim — a schema generated from `z.string().includes("foo", { position: 2 })` rejected "xxxfoo" while the validator accepted it. At `position: 0` the emitted pattern was equivalent to startsWith. The pattern reaches past JSON Schema output. It becomes the string's `_zod.pattern`, which template literals compose into their own regex, and the AOT compiler treats it as the entire check — so the compiled fast path rejected a late match and fell back to the runtime on every one. The string tests have asserted the "at or later" reading since before the pattern existed: one parses "XXXincludesXX" through `position: 2`, where the substring starts at index 3.
tasks.subject: fix(v4): let the includes(position) pattern match at or after the offset (#6024)

tasks.task: fix(v4): accept exact decimal multiples in multipleOf `z.number().multipleOf(0.07)` rejected 2.03 even though 2.03 === 29 * 0.07. Both operands round to a double before the division rounds again, so the quotient of a true decimal multiple can sit up to 1.5 of these scaled epsilons from the integer — the one-epsilon tolerance sat below its own worst case, and neighbouring multiples like 1.96 and 2.10 only passed because they happened to land inside it. Widen the tolerance to 4x. A sweep of exact decimal multiples shows no false rejections at 2x or above, and no false acceptances among clean decimal non-multiples; the small-step and scientific-notation cases from still hold.
tasks.subject: fix(v4): accept exact decimal multiples in multipleOf (#6223)

tasks.task: feat(v4): let z.nanoid() take a custom length A nanoid is 21 characters only because that is the generator's default `size`; `nanoid(10)` and `nanoid(64)` are ordinary documented calls, so the fixed `{21}` regex rejected ids real producers emit. Only the count varies — the default alphabet is exactly the 64 characters the existing class already spells — so the length rides on the def and the character class is untouched. Reworked from the original approach in this PR, which took a positional `nanoid(64)` on `z.string().nanoid()` alone. Dropping `length` from the omit list on the params type reaches every surface with no new signatures: `z.nanoid({ length })`, `zod/mini`, and the deprecated string method all work, matching how `z.uuid({ version })` and `z.url({ hostname })` already parameterize a format. The default keeps the shared regex literal rather than constructing one per schema, so an ordinary `z.nanoid()` costs no extra memory. A length that is not a positive integer now throws instead of building a regex whose braces are literal text. Zod 3 is in maintenance mode and is intentionally left untouched. Refs

tasks.task: fix: honor requestTls when proxy is SOCKS5 ProxyAgent silently dropped opts.requestTls when the configured proxy URI was socks5:// (or socks://). Socks5ProxyAgent also lacked any equivalent of requestTls, so even constructed directly it had no way to configure target HTTPS TLS settings (ca, cert, key, rejectUnauthorized, servername). The inner connect callback called tls.connect with ...connectOpts.tls || {} but undici's internal connectOpts never populates a .tls field, so the spread was a dead expression. This change: - Forwards opts.requestTls from ProxyAgent to Socks5ProxyAgent. - Adds a requestTls constructor option on Socks5ProxyAgent stored in the kRequestTls symbol. - Applies it on the inner tls.connect for the target HTTPS upgrade, with socket overriding (must point at the SOCKS5 tunnel) and servername defaulting to targetHost but allowing user override to match the HTTP-proxy path semantics. - Documents the new option in Socks5ProxyAgent.md. - Adds two regression tests covering both the direct Socks5ProxyAgent path and the ProxyAgent forwarding path. Refs GHSA-vmh5-mc38-953g

tasks.task: fix(h2): guard onResponse against a 'response' event delivered after completion * fix(h2): guard onResponse against a 'response' event delivered after completion The HTTP/2 'response' handler (onResponse) only guarded request.aborted before calling request.onResponseStart, while its sibling handlers onEnd and onTrailers also guard request.completed. A 'response' frame delivered after the request has already completed (a stream-teardown race that shows up under load on shared h2 sessions with GOAWAY / refused-stream churn) therefore calls onResponseStart post-completion, tripping its assert(!this.completed). Because it throws on the http2 stream's event tick, it surfaces as an uncaught exception and crashes the process. Add the same request.completed guard the other handlers already use. Assisted-By: devx/26cd7e09-2a13-4e79-9cd0-8191fff4dc7a * test(h2): cover 'response' delivered after request completion Regression test for the onResponse completed-guard. Drives the real onResponse handler (via connectH2) against a fake stream — mirroring test/http2-late-data.js — and emits a 'response' event after the request has completed. Without the guard this invokes request.onResponseStart, whose assert(!this.completed) throws on the http2 event tick and crashes the process; with the guard the stream is released and the event ignored. Fails against the pre-fix handler with the exact assert(!this.completed) AssertionError and passes with the fix. Refs: Assisted-By: devx/26cd7e09-2a13-4e79-9cd0-8191fff4dc7a ---------

tasks.task: fix(eventsource): enforce maxEventSize on unterminated lines The eventSource.maxEventSize limit is only checked inside parseLine(), which runs only when a line terminator (CR/LF) is reached. A server can therefore stream a data: field (or any field) that never contains a line terminator; the size check never runs and consumed chunks are never reclaimed, so the client buffers the response body without bound, driving the process toward memory exhaustion. Track the in-progress line length (currentLineSize) and reject the stream once it exceeds maxEventSize plus the longest data: field prefix. This bounds any unterminated line against the configured cap while still accepting a terminated data line whose value is exactly maxEventSize. Adds regression tests for the unterminated-line bypass (stream and E2E) and for the boundary case of a value equal to maxEventSize.

tasks.task: fix(security): defense-in-depth against already-polluted Object.prototype in formDataToJSON * fix(security): harden prototype pollution protection in formDataToJSON Replace falsy check with hasOwnProp in the intermediate-path branch of formDataToJSON's buildPath to prevent write-through into inherited objects. Without this patch, if Object.prototype is already polluted (e.g. via a third-party library or earlier vulnerability), user-supplied FormData paths like 'injected.hijack' traverse the inherited object and mutate Object.prototype in place. With hasOwnProp, the inherited slot is shadowed by a new own property, keeping writes local to the result. This is defense-in-depth: the existing __proto__ guard blocks direct prototype injection, while this change prevents exploitation of an already-polluted prototype chain. Closes * test(security): use defineProperty + toBe in prototype-pollution regression test ---------

tasks.task: perf: avoid resetting the level of request child loggers Request child loggers were created with `{ level: context.logLevel }`, which defaults to `''` unless the route sets a `logLevel` pino treats `''` as a level change (`'' !== undefined && '' !== this.level`) and calls `setLevel` with the parent's own level: That rebuilds every log method on the child and emits a `level-change` event on every request for no effect, as it still inherits the parent and ends up being a no-op semantically With the default logger enabled, this change cuts ~100 ns per request (−11.7% in-process, about −2% CPU per request end to end). A side effect is that `fastify.log` no longer emits a redundant `level-change` event for every request. Default benchmark with `logger: { level: 'info' }`: ``` ┌─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┬────────────┬────────────┬────────┐ │ Benchmark │ main │ PR │ Change │ ├─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┼────────────┼────────────┼────────┤ │ In-process request path, no sockets (median of 5) │ 827 ns/req │ 730 ns/req │ −11.7% │ ├─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┼────────────┼────────────┼────────┤ │ HTTP, autocannon -c 100 -p 10, server CPU per request (median of 8) │ 6009 ns │ 5897 ns │ −1.9% │ ├─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┼────────────┼────────────┼────────┤ │ Same run, requests/sec │ 168,627 │ 171,546 │ +1.7% │ ├─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┼────────────┼────────────┼────────┤ │ HTTP, -c 100 -p 1, server CPU per request │ 8270 ns │ 8201 ns │ −0.8% │ └─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┴────────────┴────────────┴────────┘ ```

tasks.task: fix(reply): send stream trailers after the stream actually finishes ## Checklist - [x] run `npm run test` - [x] tests are included - [ ] documentation is changed or added - [x] commit message and code follows the [Developer's Certification of Origin]( and the [Code of conduct]( ## What this does When trailers are registered, `sendStream()` pipes with `{ end: false }` so `sendTrailer()` can own `res.end()` once the trailers resolve, since the default pipe behavior would end the response on its own and race the trailer flush (`fastify.inject()` never touches a real socket, so this race never showed up in the existing tests). The trailer flush itself was wired through a plain `payload.on('end', ...)` listener. If the stream had already ended before `reply.send()` was called, that `end` event had already fired and the listener was registered too late, so the trailers never got sent, and since nothing else was calling `res.end()` either, the response hung. This moves the trailer flush into the `eos` (`stream.finished`) listener already present in `sendStream()`. It fires exactly once when the stream is done, error or not, and it fires even for a stream that finished before the listener was attached, so the pre-ended case is handled the same way as the normal one. ## Tests Added real-socket coverage in `test/reply-trailers.test.js`, since `inject()` can't see the pipe/`res.end()` race: trailers on a Readable stream, trailers on a web ReadableStream, a stream with no trailers registered, a stream that errors before ending, and a stream that has already ended before being handed to `send()`. ---------
